areas.name: McMillan Spire (West)
areas.blurb: West McMillan Spire is the taller, western summit of the twin McMillan Spires in the Southern Picket Range, first climbed via the West Ridge in 1940 by Fred and Helmy Beckey. Reported elevations vary by source (roughly 8,000-8,041 ft, e.g. Wikipedia/USGS-derived data lists 8,004 ft with 600 ft of clean prominence, while listsofjohn.com lists 8,041 ft) — typical for an interior, largely unsurveyed North Cascades summit. It is the most-climbed peak in the Southern Pickets, not because the climbing is hard (mostly class 2-3 with one short exposed step) but because the roughly 8-10 mile, 9,000+ ft approach up Goodell Creek and over Terror Basin is itself a serious undertaking. Its neighbor, East McMillan Spire (7,992 ft), sits just 0.14 mi away but requires roped rock climbing and sees far fewer ascents.

areas.name: West McMillan Spire
areas.blurb: West McMillan Spire (8,004 ft) is the higher, western summit of the twin McMillan Spires in the Southern Picket Range, deep within North Cascades National Park's Whatcom County backcountry. The peak is built of the steep granite and gneiss typical of the Pickets, rising above Terror Glacier and Terror Basin, and is reached only by a long, unmaintained approach up Goodell Creek. Fred and Helmy Beckey made the first ascent via the West Ridge on August 29, 1940, during their pioneering 1940 exploration of the Picket Range.

routes.name: Southwest Ridge
hazards: Six sustained pitches mean significantly more time on the mountain than the standard scramble, raising exposure to afternoon weather
Loose rock and route-finding uncertainty given the route's low traffic (single-digit MP ratings/photos)
Remote location with no cell coverage and a multi-hour-plus helicopter response time for rescue
routes.overview: A sustained six-pitch 5.8- alpine rock line up West McMillan Spire's southwest ridge, harder and more technical than the standard West Ridge scramble but sharing the same long approach via Terror Basin and the Terror Glacier.
routes.beta: Parties reach the east end of the Terror Glacier via the same Terror Basin approach as the West Ridge, then climb roughly six pitches of alpine rock (up to 5.8-, rated PG13) up the southwest ridge/face to the summit. Mountain Project's route page directs climbers to Beckey's Cascade Alpine Guide for further pitch-level detail; most parties climb it fully roped rather than scrambled.
routes.turnaround: Set a conditions-based turnaround rather than a fixed clock time — six roped pitches take considerably longer than the standard scramble, and afternoon thunderstorms and softening snow on the shared glacier approach add urgency to being off the ridge and back across the glacier before conditions deteriorate.
routes.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
routes.comms: No reliable cell service anywhere on the approach, in Terror Basin, or on the route; a satellite messenger (inReach/SPOT) is strongly recommended given the remoteness of the Southern Pickets.
routes.descent: Most parties descend via the easier West Ridge scramble line rather than reversing the technical rock pitches, then follow the standard Terror Basin/notch descent back to the trailhead.

timing.recommendedStart: Pre-dawn (~4-5am) alpine start from Terror Basin, given six roped pitches take longer than the standard scramble

routes.detailed_rack: A medium alpine rock rack (small-to-mid cams and a set of nuts) plus 8-10 shoulder-length runners for the long, wandering pitches, and a single ice axe for the shared glacier/snow approach.
what_to_bring: bivy/camping gear for a 2-3 day trip
approach shoes/boots suited to brush and slab
pro_tips: The final 5.8- pitch is rated PG13; climbing slightly to climber's right of the described line is reported by some as an easier variation
Beckey's Cascade Alpine Guide is the traditional reference most parties carry for this line's pitch-by-pitch detail
Plan to descend via the easier West Ridge scramble rather than reversing the technical pitches
watch_out: The crux final pitch is runout (PG13) — protection is moderate at best
Loose rock is present on the lower pitches, as on the rest of the peak
The shared glacier approach carries crevasse/moat hazard, especially early season
routes.pro_needs: Standard alpine rock protection to about 2-3 inches with extra slings to manage rope drag on wandering pitches; the crux final pitch (5.8- PG13) protects only moderately well per user notes.
routes.best_season: Late July through September, matching the West Ridge's window, once the Terror Glacier approach has consolidated; carry an ice axe for the shared glacier crossing regardless of which ridge is climbed.
routes.approach: Identical to the West Ridge approach: Goodell Creek trailhead to Terror Basin over the 6,200' notch, then traverse benches/slabs to the glacial lake outlet and up slabs onto the Terror Glacier. From there, continue to the east end of the Terror Glacier to reach the base of the southwest ridge (rather than the west-ridge gully used by the standard route).
routes.descent_text: From the summit, descend via the West Ridge's 3rd-4th class scramble and snow/ice gully back onto the Terror Glacier (rather than rappelling the southwest ridge), then re-cross the glacier and slabs to the lake outlet and climb back out over the 6,200' notch to the Goodell Creek trail.
routes.bail: Retreat by downclimbing to easier terrain and traversing off toward the West Ridge line, or by rappelling the route on gear if downclimbing is not feasible; there is no quick bail once established on the upper ridge given the surrounding Southern Pickets cliffs.

pitch_detail.notes: Lower-angle alpine rock gaining the ridge crest
Below the crux; rack up for the final pitch here

access.fees: No trailhead or parking fee; overnight backcountry camping permit costs $10/person plus a $6 reservation fee (free walk-up permits also available)

climate.spring: Heavy lingering snowpack with high avalanche/wet-slide hazard on approach slopes and the glacier; route generally not in condition
climate.summer: Prime season (Jul-Sep); afternoon thunderstorms and lightning are possible; the Terror Glacier holds firm snow into mid-summer most years
climate.winter: Not a winter objective — approach access and avalanche hazard make the route effectively closed
climate.typical: Wet, maritime North Cascades climate at lower elevations transitioning to persistent snow/glacier conditions above ~6,000'; brush and blowdown dominate the lower approach
climate.forecastZone: No dedicated summer alpine forecast zone exists; NWAC's West Slopes North zone covers this area for winter avalanche forecasting (mid-Nov to mid-Apr) only

emergency.notes: No cell coverage in Terror Basin or on route; NPS/SAR helicopter response can take many hours given the remote Southern Pickets location. Register your itinerary at the Wilderness Information Center before departure.

routes.name: West Ridge / Southwest Approach
routes.fa: Fred Beckey and Helmy Beckey, August 29, 1940
gear: 30m rope plus a light rack (a few slings/small cams or nuts) for the summit step and an optional rappel
whippet or second tool useful for firm early-season snow
hazards: loose rock, especially in the rotten red gully skier's-right of the standard descent line
steep snow (up to ~40°) and a small crevasse/moat at the 7,200 ft Inspiration-McMillan col
exposed, lightly protected class 3 step just below the true summit

routes.overview: West McMillan Spire is the taller of the twin McMillan Spires and, by Southern Picket standards, a relatively attainable summit — most parties treat it as their introduction to the range. The technical climbing itself is moderate (a snow gully to a 7,200 ft col between Inspiration Peak and West McMillan Spire, then class 2-3 ridge scrambling with one short, exposed step below the true summit), but the approach is the real crux: an overgrown, log-choked trail up Goodell Creek, an unofficial steep climber's trail onto a forested ridge, and a rising traverse into Terror Basin before the peak is even in reach. First climbed via this line in 1940 by Fred and Helmy Beckey.
routes.beta: From a high camp in Terror Basin, cross rocky benches and the Terror Glacier's outlet lake, then climb onto the glacier and pick a line to the base of the ridge. A steep snow/ice gully (steepening to roughly 40 degrees near the top) leads to the ~7,200 ft col between Inspiration Peak and West McMillan Spire. From the col, follow the west ridge over broken rock, heather, scree and talus — climbers can choose more solid rock steps or looser talus depending on preference — to a short, exposed class 3 (occasionally cited as low 5th on variations) move onto the summit block.
routes.turnaround: Set a firm turnaround time at the 7,200 ft col — the snow gully below it softens and becomes more rockfall-prone by afternoon, and the long, log-choked hike out takes several more hours after the climb.
routes.rappels: Typically down-climbed rather than rappelled — the route is descended via the same ascent line/notch gully; no fixed rappel stations are reported.
routes.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
routes.comms: Deep wilderness location in the North Cascades National Park interior with no reliable cell coverage reported by climbers; several trip reports note carrying a satellite phone/communicator as a precaution given the remoteness and multi-day rescue timelines.
routes.descent: Downclimb the west ridge back to the 7,200 ft col — a short rappel off the exposed summit step is sometimes used in low-snow years but most parties simply downclimb it. From the col, descend or glissade the snow gully back toward Terror Basin; stay skier's-left, as multiple parties have drifted right into a loose, rotten red gully by mistake. Reverse the traverse back to Terror Basin camp, then retrace the climber's trail and the overgrown Goodell Creek trail to the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek Campground / Trailhead

waypoints.name: Treeline / heather benches

waypoints.name: Terror Basin camp
waypoints.note: Gravelly wildflower basin with several small streams; the established tent sites here are the standard base camp, roughly 3:15 in from the trailhead.

waypoints.name: The Barrier traverse
waypoints.note: Serious class-3 crossing of the ridge separating Terror Creek and Crescent Creek basins via a steep, loose grassy ledge (~6,100 ft) up to the crest (~6,400 ft); heavily exposed, loose rock, described by climbers as a 'slip-and-die' section.

waypoints.name: Crescent Creek basin / 7,200 ft col
waypoints.note: After descending into Crescent Creek basin, heather/snow/rock leads back up to this col on the west ridge — the same col used again on the downclimb per the on-file descent.

waypoints.name: West McMillan Spire summit

routes.detailed_rack: A technical rack is optional rather than mandatory. Most parties carry an ice axe and crampons for the Terror Glacier crossing and the snow/ice gully to the col, plus a helmet for loose rock above. Some parties bring a light rope and a small rack of cams/nuts to protect the short exposed class 3 (occasionally low 5th) step below the summit block, but many climb the entire route unroped.
what_to_bring: 30m rope and a light rack for the summit step
bear canister (recommended for Terror Basin camp)
pro_tips: Camp at Terror Basin (~5,800 ft) rather than attempting a single push; it has flat gravel tent sites and running water and turns the summit day into just a few hours round trip.
Budget 2-4 hours for the first 4 miles along Goodell Creek alone due to deadfall — don't judge pace on mileage.
Carry a satellite communicator; there is no cell coverage anywhere on this route.
watch_out: Stay skier's-left descending the col gully — drifting right drops parties into a loose, rotten red gully that has caught out multiple groups.
The col crevasse/moat and the steep (~40°) snow below it can be firm and icy in early morning; a slip here has a long runout.
The Goodell Creek approach trail is unmaintained — 100+ downed logs and a couple of washouts make the first 4 miles far slower than the mileage suggests.
routes.pro_needs: Minimal protection needed overall — a light rack of a few slings/small cams or nuts covers the short 5.6/class-3 step near the summit; the rope is mostly for security and an optional short rappel rather than sustained pitched climbing.
routes.best_season: Late July through September is the reliable snow-manageable window (most recorded trip reports climb between late July and late August). June and early-July ascents are a genuinely more technical snow/ice climb, with firmer, steeper névé in the gully below the col (documented on a June 6, 2023 ascent) — not recommended without solid snow-climbing skills. By late September/October fresh snow can return to the ridge and gully, adding difficulty and cutting daylight short on an already long day.
routes.approach: From the Goodell Creek (Upper Group Campground) trailhead just east of Goodell Creek Campground off SR-20 near Newhalem, pick up the unsigned climbers'-path (no trail number — this is a boot path, not a maintained Park trail) that starts behind a large boulder near the campground. There is reliable running water right at the start, then none again until Terror Basin, so top off bottles early. The path switchbacks up through second-growth and old-growth forest along a spur ridge south of Terror Creek and is notorious for blowdown — expect to climb over or duck under dozens of downed logs for the first couple of miles. Around 3,200 ft the trail gains the crest of the forested ridge and settles into a steady, unrelenting climb (roughly 4,000 ft of gain over about 2 miles is typical for this stretch). Near 4,000 ft it crosses a small talus field, circles left, and makes a rising traverse beneath a rock band at about 4,800 ft before kicking up a final steep gully. From there, heather benches and open slabs lead north for a couple of miles, with blueberries in late summer, to a notch in the ridge crest at roughly 6,200-6,350 ft — the high point of the approach. The north side of this notch is the crux of the approach, not the climb: in late-season/low-snow conditions it is steep, loose, chossy terrain for about 400 vertical feet (stay skier's-right — going straight down is a bad idea); early in the season it holds a firmer snow finger with a short, steeper headwall (reported up to ~80 degrees for the last 20-30 ft) that some parties rope up for or protect with a short lower. Below the notch, a small flat gravelly basin near 5,800 ft with running water is the standard Terror Basin camp. From camp, a long traverse over benches and granite slabs, trending slightly downhill, reaches a glacial lake outlet and then slabs below the Terror Glacier remnant; the glacier crossing is short and low-angle but can show bare ice by late summer — most parties cross unroped in stable conditions with crampons on. This leads to the base of the snow/rock gully that climbs to the 7,200 ft col between Inspiration Peak and West McMillan Spire, where the technical climbing begins. One-way distance from car to high camp is roughly 8-9 miles with 6,000+ ft of gain; a fit, loaded party should plan on 6-8+ hours.
routes.descent_text: This route is descended by reversing the line of ascent essentially top to bottom — there is no separate walk-off. From the summit, downclimb the short, exposed Class 3 rock back down to the base of the summit block, then descend the snow/rock gully to the 7,200 ft Inspiration-McMillan col, following the same snow finger climbed on the way up. That finger is glissade-able in soft, sun-affected afternoon snow, but if it is firm or icy (common in the morning or early season) parties often belay the downclimb or make a single short rappel/lower instead — one rope length is plenty (a single 30m section has been reported as sufficient), off natural anchors since there is nothing bolted or fixed on this route: a sling around a rock horn on the rock steps near the col, or a snow bollard/picket if the finger itself is icy. From the col, recross the Terror Glacier remnant and the granite benches back toward Terror Basin, then climb back up to the ridge notch and descend its loose, chossy north-side gully into the Goodell Creek drainage (same skier's-right line used on approach — avoid going straight down). From there it's a straightforward but long retrace of the forested trail, roughly 4 miles through the blowdown-choked lower section, back to the Goodell Creek trailhead. Total descent is on the order of 8,000-10,000 ft of elevation loss. The one rappel/protected-lower point is condition-dependent — more likely needed early season or in icy conditions on the snow finger or notch headwall — rather than a fixed technical rappel every party makes.
routes.bail: Retreat is back over the Barrier; manageable but long.

Cross the glacial lake outlet, ascend slabs onto Terror Glacier, pick a line to the base of the West Ridge.

pitch_detail.notes: Mostly scree, talus and broken rock with route-finding choice between solid rock and looser talus; a short exposed step gains the summit block.

itinerary.cal: Terror Basin is typically climbed July-September once the approach trail is snow-free and the Terror Glacier snow finger is filled in but not yet fully melted out/icy; North Cascades NP backcountry camping requires a permit for Terror Basin.

days.note: From the Goodell Creek trailhead (600 ft), follow the old forestry-road bed roughly 4 miles through mossy, brushy, deadfall-choked forest, then turn uphill at the cairned junction for a steep 2-mile, ~4,000 ft climb through heather benches and blueberry fields to the notch overlooking Terror Basin. A short, occasionally exposed scramble drops into the basin, where most parties camp on rock slabs/meadows near water below Terror, Degenhardt, Inspiration and the McMillan Spires.

Most parties are back in camp by early-to-mid afternoon after a leisurely 4-5 hour round trip.

itinerary.totalNote: A 3-day, 2-night trip is the standard plan: ~4.5 mi/5,300 ft to Terror Basin camp, a ~4 mi/2,300 ft round-trip summit day via the Terror Glacier snow finger and West Ridge, and a ~4.5 mi/5,400 ft hike out — call it ~9,800 ft gain and ~16 miles round trip overall, matching the on-file stats.
itinerary.sourceNote: Based on Eric's Base Camp trip report (ericsbasecamp.net/trips/TerrorBasin) which documents the classic 2-night/3-day structure (trailhead to camp in ~5.5 hr, summit day with ~2,200 ft round trip, then exit), the WTA route description of the Terror Basin approach and glacier/west-ridge crossing, and the on-file itinerary text. Note very fit parties can compress this to a single very long car-to-car day (ClimberKyle.com logged ~10 hr / 20 mi car-to-car) or a fast 2-ski-mountaineering day (turns-all-year.com, April conditions), but those are not the standard approach given the notoriously slow, deadfall-choked, route-finding-heavy approach trail — most parties budget 2 nights as a weather/rest buffer, per the on-file note. Clock times on the summit-day schedule are reasonable estimates from typical Terror Basin trip-report pacing, not a single verbatim source.

access.fees: $10 per person per night plus a $6 non-refundable reservation/permit fee during the summer season (mid-May through early October); climbers 15 and under are free. No day-use or trailhead parking fee.
access.notes: 60% of sites are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Camp only within your permitted Terror Basin zone site; no campfires above treeline; pack out all waste and food scraps; a bear canister is recommended for the basin camp.
access.permit: A backcountry camping permit is required for any overnight stay in the Terror Basin cross-country zone — reserve ahead on Recreation.gov or get a walk-up permit at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount. No permit is required for a single-push day climb (rare given the approach length).
access.closures: SR 20 (North Cascades Highway) closes for winter between the Ross Dam trailhead (MP 134) and Silver Star Gate (MP 171); the Goodell Creek/Newhalem trailhead sits west of that closure and is normally open year-round. However, closures have moved further west to the Newhalem gate (MP 120) in severe years, and after a December 2025 atmospheric-river storm the highway was closed all the way to Newhalem into mid-June 2026 for repairs — always check WSDOT road conditions before a trip.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park Complex (NPS) — Wilderness Information Center, Marblemount, WA; (360) 854-7245.
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)

road.name: Goodell Creek Campground access off SR 20 (North Cascades Highway)
road.status: Open in typical summer conditions; sits west of the usual winter SR 20 closure gate at Ross Dam (MP 134).
road.driveNote: Paved to the trailhead; small unpaved parking area fills early on summer weekends.
road.seasonalGate: No gate at the trailhead itself in most years, but the closure boundary has moved as far west as Newhalem (MP 120) in severe years — confirm current status with WSDOT before driving out.

climate.typical: Big diurnal swings are typical: warm, sun-exposed scrambling on the ridge by midday, but near-freezing temperatures and firm snow at the 7,200 ft col in early morning. Afternoon thunderstorm build-up is common on hot August days in the North Cascades interior, so an early start matters.

bySeason.fall: By mid/late September fresh snow can reappear on the ridge and in the gully, and shortening daylight makes the long approach and descent tighter — watch NWS mountain forecasts closely.
bySeason.spring: Snow-covered into late June/early July most years; a June ascent is a genuine technical snow/ice climb up steeper, firmer névé to the col rather than the class 2-3 scramble it becomes later in the season.
bySeason.summer: Late July through August is the most reliable window — the snow gully to the col typically softens by midday and the ridge/summit step are usually snow-free.
bySeason.winter: Effectively inaccessible: SR 20 typically closes for the season in early December, and the route itself sits in serious avalanche terrain.

climate.forecastZone: NWS Zone WAZ301 (Cascades of Whatcom & Skagit Counties) is the relevant mountain-weather zone; NWAC does not forecast avalanche danger for the Pickets and only operates roughly mid-November through June anyway.

emergency.notes: There is no cell coverage anywhere in the Pickets; the nearest reliable signal is back near Marblemount/Rockport on SR 20. A satellite communicator (inReach/Zoleo) is strongly recommended given the remoteness and multi-hour-to-multi-day SAR response time for this zone.
emergency.rangerStation: North Cascades National Park - Wilderness Information Center, Marblemount, WA; (360) 854-7245.
emergency.nearestHospital: PeaceHealth United General Medical Center, Sedro-Woolley, WA
emergency.sheriffDispatch: Whatcom County Sheriff's Office coordinates ground search-and-rescue for this area in cooperation with NPS wilderness rangers; dial 911 for emergencies.

crowds.peakTraffic: Rare cluster during peak conditions in late July-August; essentially solitude the rest of the season
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Very low — likely fewer than 10-20 parties per season

fitnessSpec.hiking: Very strenuous, largely off-trail approach through the Barrier and into Crescent Creek/Terror Basin; typically a 2-day approach each way with sustained bushwhacking and route-finding before the technical climbing even starts
fitnessSpec.packWeight: 40-45+ lb overnight pack for the approach; trip reports note faster summit pushes (~4.5 hrs camp-to-camp) once camp is established

partner_requirements.approachTime: ~2 days approach (trailhead to Crescent Creek/Terror Basin camp); summit day itself roughly 4-6 hrs camp-to-camp per trip reports
requiredSkills: Off-trail route-finding in trailless, remote terrain (the Barrier crossing is a known crux, especially in poor visibility)
Snow/glacier travel and self-arrest for the approach and summit snow finger
Low 5th class rock climbing (5.6) with sustained exposure near the summit block
Multi-day backcountry camping and self-sufficiency (North Cascades NP wilderness permit required)
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Experienced alpine climbers only — this is not a beginner objective; requires prior multi-day glacier/alpine approach experience plus comfort on low 5th-class rock with real exposure and no rescue nearby

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through September, with late July-August the most reliable stretch (consistent with existing best_season)

July.reason: Early July can still hold lingering snow in approach gullies with moats forming on the summit snow finger; conditions consolidate through the month

August.reason: Most stable window — snow finger typically intact but manageable, dry rock on the ridge, and the most predictable weather of the season

September.reason: Generally dry rock but shorter days and rising chance of early-season storms or new snow at elevation late in the month

weather.typical: Remote alpine climate; cold and storm-prone outside the midsummer window, snowbound in spring, severe and rarely attempted in winter (per existing climate data)
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms and fast-moving North Cascades weather systems are common in summer; the exposed summit block and ridge crest raise lightning and fall-in-a-storm risk

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Significant exposure on the summit block and along the upper west ridge scramble; a fall there would be severe. The Barrier crossing in poor visibility (already flagged on file) adds route-finding and fall hazard on the approach itself

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer scramble/climb; outside NWAC's forecast zones and season (NWAC does not issue forecasts for the North Cascades NP backcountry in summer)

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: The standard approach and descent cross the Terror Glacier remnant near the 7,200 ft Inspiration-McMillan col, where a small crevasse/moat forms - the crossing is short and low-angle and most parties cross unroped in stable conditions with crampons, but it is not off-route and should not be assumed crevasse-free.

gaps: Exact prominence is disputed between sources (600 ft per Wikipedia vs. 737 ft on file) — left unchanged pending an authoritative survey source.
No confirmed pitch count or protection rating exists for the summit step; treated as a short scramble/optional-rope move, not graded pitches.
No NWAC or other authoritative avalanche/snow-condition forecast covers this zone; current conditions should be sourced from recent trip reports (CascadeClimbers, WTA) before a trip.

routes.name: Southwest Ridge
hazards: Remote Southern Pickets setting means any rescue is slow and difficult.
Loose rock is characteristic of Picket Range ridgelines generally.
routes.overview: A longer, more technical trad line up the southwest side of West McMillan Spire, rated 5.8- over 6 pitches (Grade III), in contrast to the scrambling West Ridge.
routes.beta: Documented on Mountain Project with a grade and rack but almost no route-finding beta; the page explicitly directs climbers to Fred Beckey's Cascade Alpine Guide ('the red guidebook') for the actual pitch-by-pitch description. Shares the same remote Southern Pickets approach zone (Goodell Creek to Terror Basin/Terror Glacier) as the West Ridge, though the exact line taken to reach the base of the ridge from the glacier is not detailed in available online sources.
routes.turnaround: Given the multi-day, glacier-guarded approach and limited published beta, parties should set a conservative turnaround based on remaining daylight, weather trends, and rock conditions rather than pushing into terrain they cannot down-climb or retreat from safely.
routes.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
routes.comms: No cell service in this remote wilderness area; a satellite communicator or PLB is strongly recommended given the multi-day approach and glacier travel.
routes.descent: Reverse the route; down-climb/rappel the ridge and re-cross Terror Glacier back to Terror Basin camp.

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek Trailhead/Campground
waypoints.note: Standard access for all Southern Pickets climbs (McMillan Spires, Inspiration Peak, Mt Terror, etc.) via the unmaintained Goodell Creek climber's path, gaining ~4700ft into Terror Basin. Same trailhead used for both routes on this peak.

timing.recommendedStart: Alpine start from Terror Basin camp to allow time for the glacier crossing and technical climbing before typical afternoon weather buildup.

routes.detailed_rack: Mountain Project recommends a medium alpine rock rack with 8-10 runners, a helmet, and a single ice axe for the glacier/snow approach.
what_to_bring: extra layers for exposed ridge climbing
pro_tips: Online beta for this route is sparse; consult Fred Beckey's Cascade Alpine Guide for the actual route description before attempting it, as Mountain Project itself defers to that guidebook.
watch_out: Loose rock on multiple pitches, consistent with Pickets granite/gneiss — helmet essential.
Retreat options are limited once established on the ridge; this is committing alpine terrain far from help.
routes.pro_needs: Medium alpine rock rack with 8-10 runners, a helmet, and one ice axe (per Mountain Project route page).
routes.best_season: Summer climbing window, roughly June through September, consistent with the broader Southern Pickets climbing season documented in trip reports for this peak; specific season data for this exact line was not found beyond that general window.
routes.approach: From the Goodell Creek Campground trailhead near Newhalem, climbers follow an unmaintained, boot-worn path roughly 4 to 4.5 miles up the forested Goodell Creek valley before turning uphill on a brutally steep, brushy side path that gains around 1,500 feet in well under half a mile. Above treeline the route makes a rising traverse across heather and scree to a notch near 6,200 feet overlooking Terror Basin, which serves as the standard base camp. From camp, reaching West McMillan Spire itself requires crossing a permanent snowfield/glacier remnant (crampons and an ice axe are mandatory) before finishing on exposed Class 2-3 scrambling to the summit. This is a genuine multi-day expedition-style approach; a North Cascades National Park backcountry permit is required, and there is significant routefinding and rockfall/glacier hazard throughout.
routes.bail: Limited fixed bail options on the ridge itself; the safest retreat is down-climbing/rappelling back the way you came to the glacier before committing above hard-to-reverse pitches.
routes.itinerary: Typically a 2-3 day trip: Day 1 approach to Terror Basin camp (6-8 hrs); Day 2 climb the Southwest Ridge and return to camp; Day 3 hike out via Goodell Creek.

climate.winter: Deep snowpack and avalanche terrain make the route effectively inaccessible to climbers.

routes.corrections: Route name, grade, and type verified on Mountain Project; specific rack sizes not published in any trip report found.
rack: 1 snow picket + ice axe for approach

routes.name: West Ridge
hazards: Terror Glacier crossing carries crevasse and glacier-travel hazard even though it is typically done unroped.
The summit ridge is narrow and heavily exposed, with large cliffs on both sides in places.
Rockfall and loose rock are recurring themes in trip reports of this route.
Weather can deteriorate quickly this deep in the Picket Range, complicating the long retreat.
routes.overview: The classic and most-climbed route on West McMillan Spire: a long glacier and scramble approach from Terror Basin over Terror Glacier, up a steep snow/ice gully to gain the West Ridge, then a 3rd-4th class scramble along scree, talus, and an exposed summit ridge to the summit block.
routes.beta: From a Terror Basin camp, cross rocky benches and the outlet of a glacial lake, climb slabs and snow onto Terror Glacier below the McMillan Spires, then ascend a steep snow/ice gully to reach the crest of the West Ridge. From there it is a mellow but exposed 3rd-4th class scramble up scree and talus to the summit block. The glacier crossing is normally done unroped but crampons and an ice axe are standard; some parties encounter thin, hollow snow over rock and short mixed moves on the upper ridge, especially in a low-snow year.
routes.turnaround: Because the descent retraces steep snow/ice and loose, exposed scrambling terrain, parties should set a firm turnaround time based on remaining daylight and building afternoon weather, and should not linger on the summit ridge if clouds or thunderstorms are developing.
routes.rappels: Not typically roped for rappel — the route is usually downclimbed/scrambled in reverse; a single rope is sufficient if any short rappels are needed on loose sections.
routes.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
routes.comms: No cell service in this remote wilderness area; carry a satellite communicator or PLB — this is frequently cited as one of the most remote areas in the Lower 48.
routes.descent: Reverse the West Ridge route back down the snow/ice gully to Terror Glacier and Terror Basin.

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek Trailhead/Campground
waypoints.note: Same Goodell Creek approach into Terror Basin as Southwest Ridge; West Ridge is the more popular/moderate (4th class) line and is climbed from the same basin.

timing.recommendedStart: Pre-dawn alpine start from the Terror Basin camp (trip reports describe leaving camp around 3:30-4:00 AM) to cross the glacier while snow is firm and clear the summit ridge before afternoon weather.

routes.detailed_rack: Not a rock climb in the traditional sense - the technical crux is a steep snow/ice gully and short mixed moves near the false summit. Ice axe and crampons are standard; some parties carry a short rope and a few slings for the gully and the exposed summit block scramble, though most ascents are done unroped.
what_to_bring: bivy/camping gear for a 2-3 day trip
water treatment (no reliable water source between the top of the hillclimb and Terror Basin)
sturdy mountaineering boots suited to scrambling and snow travel
navigation (map/GPS/compass) for the unmarked, unmaintained approach trail
bear canister if required for the camping zone
pro_tips: Find the correct trailhead: use the unmarked trail on the east side of Goodell Creek across from the Visitor Center sign, not the Goodell Creek Campground sign on the west side.
Terror Basin is the standard bivy - flat spots and running water, but no water between the top of the initial hillclimb and the basin itself.
Carry ice axe and crampons even late in the season; multiple trip reports describe using them for the glacier crossing and gully despite it being a relatively 'easy' 8,000-footer.
A helmet is recommended near the notch/section between Inspiration Peak and McMillan Spire due to looseness.
watch_out: Hundreds of blowdowns litter the unmaintained lower climbers' trail.
The gully and upper ridge can hold thin, hollow snow over rock, especially late season - probe before committing.
Reddish rock near the summit approach is described as poor quality/deteriorating.
The north-side notch descent without snow cover is steep, loose choss - stay skier's right.
routes.pro_needs: Crampons and an ice axe are required for the Terror Glacier crossing and the snow/ice gully to the ridge crest (per Mountain Project).
routes.best_season: Roughly June through September based on documented ascents (trip reports span early June to late August/September). Earlier-season trips have more continuous snow for the glacier crossing and gully (requiring axe and crampons throughout), while by late summer the glacier surface softens, the gully can be melted out to loose scree, and rockfall/looseness increases with warming.
routes.approach: From the Goodell Creek Campground trailhead near Newhalem, climbers follow an unmaintained, boot-worn path roughly 4 to 4.5 miles up the forested Goodell Creek valley before turning uphill on a brutally steep, brushy side path that gains around 1,500 feet in well under half a mile. Above treeline the route makes a rising traverse across heather and scree to a notch near 6,200 feet overlooking Terror Basin, which serves as the standard base camp. From camp, reaching West McMillan Spire itself requires crossing a permanent snowfield/glacier remnant (crampons and an ice axe are mandatory) before finishing on exposed Class 2-3 scrambling to the summit. This is a genuine multi-day expedition-style approach; a North Cascades National Park backcountry permit is required, and there is significant routefinding and rockfall/glacier hazard throughout.
routes.descent_text: Downclimb the exposed 3rd-4th class summit ridge and scree/talus back to the top of the steep snow/ice gully, then descend the gully (facing in if icy) back onto Terror Glacier. Recross the glacier and benches to Terror Basin camp, then reverse the steep, loose, brushy climbers' trail back to Goodell Creek. Some parties note the north-side notch descent without snow cover is intimidating steep loose choss and recommend staying skier's right.
routes.bail: The technical crux is the steep snow/ice gully between the glacier and the ridge crest; below that, retreat is a straightforward reversal of scrambling terrain. If conditions in the gully deteriorate (ice, rockfall), parties can retreat back across Terror Glacier and out via Terror Basin rather than continuing to the ridge.

pitch_detail.notes: Steep snow/ice gully gains the West Ridge crest from the glacier; crampons and axe required, occasionally roped depending on conditions.
Scree and talus scrambling along the ridge.
Exposed summit block scramble to the true summit.

routes.itinerary: Day 1: Drive to Goodell Creek trailhead and hike the steep, brushy climbers' trail (~5,000 ft gain) to a bivy at Terror Basin (~5,800 ft). Day 2: Pre-dawn alpine start; cross benches and the glacial lake outlet, ascend slabs/snow onto Terror Glacier, climb the steep snow/ice gully to the West Ridge crest, and scramble 3rd-4th class terrain to the summit; reverse the route back to Terror Basin camp. Day 3: Hike out to the trailhead.
